newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Sarajevo infrastructure fair bustles with business.
newsitem.headline: Sarajevo infrastructure fair bustles with business.

text.p: Foreign and Bosnian companies descended on a Sarajevo exhibition hall on Tuesday in search of business opportunities in reconstructing Bosnia's war-shattered infrastructure.

More than 500 foreign and local companies attended the fair devoted to Bosnia's infrastructure rebuilding and organised by the London-based International Trade and Exhibition Group (ITE) and Skenderija, a massive sports complex that includes the stadium where the fair is being held.
The primary goal of the exhibition was establishing trading links between foreign and local firms after the devastating 1992-1995 war.

"This is yet another proof that foreign companies are interested in cooperation with local companies and that they want to see us in their businesses," Skenderija's director Sadik Hasanbegovic said in his opening speech.
The international community has committed more than one billion dollars to reconstruct the country's devastated infrastructure since fighting ended with a peace accord in November 1995.

But international donors have urged authorities to adopt market-oriented legislation, carry out privatisation and approve a package of basic economic reforms to clear the way for more aid and investment.
For companies such as Swedish truck-maker Scania, the fair was an opportunity to cautiously probe Bosnia's politically volatile market.

"Scania is a very conservative company and we are never the first ones to rush in," Lennart Persson, the company's southern Europe sales manager, said. "This is our fifth visit since the war ended and now we are looking at opening an office in Sarajevo," he said.

Persson said Scania will be looking into internationally funded reconstruction projects for possible business opportunities but will also target Bosnian companies with a presentation tour around the country next week.
"There is a tremendous need for transport and now we feel that the war risk has been minimalised. We think that now is the time to come and start a slow-growing presence," he said.

Spread across three sport halls that hosted ice-skating competitions during the 1984 Winter Olympic games, companies displayed construction, power, water, transportation, telecommunications and health care products.
Siemens and Asea Brown Boveri (ABB) were clearly vying to win contracts for restoring Bosnia's power network, which was heavily damaged in the 1992-1995 war.

"Now that the climate in which the state protected local power equipment suppliers has changed, it is possible to win major power contracts in Bosnia," said Namik Hadzi-Ibrahimovic, ABB's Bosnia representative.
"This exhibition will enable me to introduce this company to businessmen from smaller cities where there is potential to service small industrial facilities."
Although the Sarajevo exhibition had attracted big interest, most foreign companies were hesitant to launch direct investment in Bosnia.

"Very few (foreign companies) would be spending a lot of their own money, they will look for the opportunity for a World Bank project," Philip Watkins, from the private consulting firm Resolution Partnership, said.
"There are certainly big possibilities but it's the political stability that everyone is looking for."
